summary: A new recommendation model was released behind a feature flag at 2% traffic exposure and produced incorrect results for one low-volume customer segment. Segment-level quality monitoring detected a 14-point precision drop six minutes after exposure, which exceeded the automated release rule's 5-point halt threshold, and the flag was disabled for the affected segment while the previous model continued serving all other traffic. Total affected requests were 312 and no other segment showed a measurable quality drop. The defect escaped pre-release integration tests, which all passed. The evidence establishes the containment sequence and its scale, but does not state the mechanism of the defect, the elapsed time from detection to disablement, or whether the halt and the disablement were automated or human actions.

claims.statement: The new recommendation model produced incorrect results for exactly one low-volume customer segment after deployment.
Exposure was limited by design: the release began at 2% of traffic behind a feature flag.
Segment-level (not aggregate-only) quality monitoring was in place and surfaced the regression six minutes after exposure.
The observed 14-point precision drop exceeded the automated release rule's 5-point per-segment halt threshold by a wide margin.
The automated rule's trigger condition was met, so expansion of the release beyond 2% was halted.
Remediation was scoped to the affected segment only; the previous model kept serving all other traffic rather than a full rollback.
Total customer impact was bounded at 312 requests, with no measurable quality drop in any other segment.
The pre-release integration test suite did not detect the defect: the artifact passed all of its tests.
The failure was detected in production by runtime monitoring rather than by pre-release verification.
The team had rehearsed the specific remediation mechanism used (feature-flag rollback) in the previous month.
The layered controls in combination — limited exposure, segment-level monitoring, a threshold rule, and a flag-based off switch — bounded the blast radius of a defect that verification did not catch.
The evidence describes containment of the incident but never states the underlying cause of the incorrect results.

relationships.note: Capping exposure at 2% limited the population that could be served incorrect results.
The defective behavior existed before monitoring registered the precision drop.
Detection of the drop is what supplies the rule its trigger input.
The magnitude of the drop exceeded the stated halt threshold.
Halting expansion kept exposure from growing beyond the initial 2%.
Detection preceded disabling the flag for the segment; the evidence does not state the interval.
Disabling the flag for the affected segment ended the accrual of affected requests.
Segment-scoped disablement is the mechanism by which impact stayed confined to one segment.
Prior rehearsal plausibly eased execution of the flag rollback; no timing evidence confirms an effect.
A verification gap allowed a defective artifact to reach production traffic.
Tests passing while production monitoring caught the issue locates detection downstream of verification.
Absence of drops elsewhere supports segment-specific rather than global defect.
A pre-declared quantitative threshold is one of the layered controls.
The feature flag used for gradual exposure was also the control used to remove exposure.
The causal mechanism linking the new model to segment-specific incorrect results is not established by any evidence item.
Whether the 312 requests accrued mainly before detection, between detection and disablement, or across both is not stated.

uncertainties.statement: The cause of the incorrect results is unknown — data skew, insufficient training representation of a low-volume segment, a feature-pipeline mismatch, or something else.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A root-cause analysis of the model's behavior on the affected segment, including its training-data composition and serving-time feature values.

uncertainties.statement: Whether the halt (E4) and the flag disablement (E5) were executed automatically by the release system or manually by an operator is not stated.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The release-automation configuration and the audit log of who or what issued the halt and flag change.

uncertainties.statement: The elapsed time between detection at six minutes and disablement of the flag is not given, so response latency cannot be assessed.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Timestamps for the detection alert and the flag-disable action.

uncertainties.statement: Why the integration tests passed is unknown — no evidence describes their coverage of segment-level quality or of this segment specifically.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The pre-release test suite's contents and coverage report, in particular whether it evaluated per-segment precision.

uncertainties.statement: Whether the 312 affected requests produced real customer harm, and of what kind, is not stated; 'incorrect results' is not quantified as impact.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Downstream outcome data for those requests (customer complaints, conversion, support tickets) or a defined harm model.

uncertainties.statement: Whether monitoring would have detected a similar regression in an even smaller or differently defined segment is unknown; segment definitions and detection sensitivity are not described.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The monitoring system's segment taxonomy and its minimum sample size or statistical power per segment.

uncertainties.statement: Whether the practiced rollback (E8) materially changed the response is not established; there is no comparison point.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Response-time data for flag rollbacks before and after the practice exercise.

uncertainties.statement: The current state of the release is not stated — whether the model still serves the other 2%-eligible segments, and whether a fix or full rollback followed.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The post-incident release status and flag configuration.

actions.statement: Perform and document a root-cause analysis for the affected segment before any further exposure of this model; C12 and U1 show the incident is contained but not explained.
Add per-segment quality checks to pre-release verification so the class of defect caught only in production (C9) has a chance to fail earlier.
Record the detection-to-disablement timeline and the 312-request accrual curve, so the response-latency component of blast radius can be measured rather than assumed.
Confirm whether the halt and disablement were automated; if either required a human, treat that as the limiting factor on response time under a higher-volume segment.
Review monitoring sensitivity for low-volume segments, since the defect landed in one and detection power there is unverified.
Retain the layered control set (limited exposure, segment monitoring, threshold rule, flag rollback) and the rollback practice cadence as deliberate practice, not incidental.

counterfactuals.statement: Had monitoring been aggregate-only rather than segment-level, a 14-point drop confined to one low-volume segment would plausibly have been diluted below any alert threshold and gone undetected for far longer.
Had the release gone to 100% of traffic instead of 2%, affected requests would have been far greater than 312, scaling roughly with the exposed share of that segment's volume.
Had the halt threshold been set above 14 points rather than 5, the rule would not have fired and expansion could have continued.
Had no segment-scoped feature flag existed, remediation would have required a coarser action — a full rollback or redeploy — affecting traffic that was serving correctly.
Had the defect affected a high-volume segment instead, the same six-minute detection latency would have yielded substantially more than 312 affected requests.
Had the integration tests included per-segment quality assertions, the defect might have been caught pre-release; this depends on U1's unknown cause being reproducible in a test environment.
